title: Teli: oil, transport and changing work
description: Teli community history in Odisha through oil pressing, pack-bullock transport, regional names and a dated village example of work beyond inherited occupations.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: What can an occupation tell us about a community’s history—and where does it stop explaining an individual life? For Teli history in Odisha, the useful questions concern work, regional names and the evidence behind accounts of origin.

paragraphs.text: The 1909 Telli entry by Edgar Thurston, assisted by K. Rangachari, connects Odia oil pressers with Holodia, Bolodia and Khadi sections, cautiously describing that division as apparent. It associates Bolodia with carrying produce on pack bullocks and Khadi chiefly with pressing oil, while acknowledging that others also pressed it. Holodia turmeric cultivation and sale appear as a reported earlier occupation, not a dated origin.

Its account of document marks is especially concrete. People signing by a nisani could use a turmeric symbol, a bullock’s belt or the oil mill’s curved pole, associated respectively with those three sections. Work could therefore enter a document through a recognisable object.
paragraphs.locator: Printed16; interpretation of recorded document marks

paragraphs.text: The same account describes women collecting wedding water from seven houses, with conch and pipe accompaniment, and identifies water collection as shared with other Odia communities. This is a historical description, not a rule for every family today.

sections.title: The regional accounts do not match neatly

paragraphs.text: The Bhadrak District Gazetteer gives a different arrangement: Haladia and Khari are associated with oil pressing, while Baladia or Thoria are linked to transporting turmeric by bullock. It also describes movement into trade, manufacture and other professions. These descriptions belong to the gazetteer’s account; they are not a current employment survey.

The difference matters. We should retain each source’s names, place and account of work rather than combine them into one fixed branch chart. Neither account establishes that everybody with a related name followed the same occupation.

A village study offers a small but useful counterexample to treating inherited occupation as destiny. The Daanla monograph, part of the 1961 Census series, was investigated in 1962 and published in 1968. In this Keonjhar village it recorded one Teli resident: the schoolteacher. Its settlement account places his arrival within the generation then living.
One resident cannot represent a community’s employment across Odisha. He does show why a community label and a person’s actual work need to be recorded separately.
paragraphs.locator: Interpretation limited to the single surveyed resident

paragraphs.text: Bhadrak’s account records Kuberaputra, meaning sons of Kubera, as a name associated with the community. That religious association is part of the naming tradition; it does not establish a historical genealogy or date of formation.
paragraphs.locator: Printed43; tradition distinguished from historical evidence

paragraphs.text: The inspected sources do not identify a single founder or an occasion when the community was created. A fuller history needs local records and attributed family accounts alongside descriptions of occupation. Names such as Sahu or Sahoo cannot, on their own, establish somebody’s caste.
